← Security questionnaire answer matcher

How to answer a customer security questionnaire faster

Before a business buys software, its security team often sends a spreadsheet of a hundred or more questions. The questions differ in wording but cover the same ground, so the fastest approach is to write each answer once, keep it somewhere approved, and reuse it. The risk is reusing an answer that no longer fits the question. This guide covers both halves.

Match a questionnaire against your saved answers

Build the library

  • Start from the last questionnaire you answered. Save each question and the answer you gave, one row each, as a two-column CSV.
  • Cover the recurring topics: access control and MFA, encryption at rest and in transit, incident response and notification windows, backups and restore tests, penetration testing, vulnerability management, subprocessors, employee screening and training, compliance reports, data retention and deletion.
  • Put figures in the answer. "Within 72 hours" is checkable next time; "promptly" is not.
  • Date each answer in a tags column so stale ones are easy to find.

Before you reuse an answer

  • Compare the numbers. A question asking for a 24-hour notification and an answer promising 72 are close in wording and opposite in meaning.
  • Watch negations. "Do you allow X?" and "Do you not allow X?" take opposite yes/no answers.
  • Check scope. An answer about your production environment may not hold for support tooling or a customer-specific deployment.
  • Check that it is still true. A pen test from two years ago is not "annual".

Mistakes that come back later

  • Answers that contradict a contract, a trust page or a previous customer's sheet.
  • Promising controls you plan to have rather than controls you have.
  • Several people answering the same topic differently.
  • Pasting a long policy where a one-line yes/no was asked.

Doing the first pass in seconds

The free matcher runs in your browser. It compares each incoming question with your saved questions, folds synonyms such as MFA and two-factor, shows a confidence level, flags changed figures and negations, and lists the questions you still have to write answers for. It is a heuristic: it suggests, you decide. Related tools: SOC 2 readiness checker, security headers check and RFP compliance matrix generator.

Common questions

How long should a security questionnaire take to answer?

The first one is slow because nothing is written down. After that most rows repeat: encryption, access control, incident response, backups, subprocessors, and compliance reports recur in nearly every customer's sheet. Keeping approved answers in one library and reusing them turns most of a questionnaire into review rather than writing.

Who should approve security questionnaire answers?

One named owner, usually the security lead or the founder at a small company, so that answers do not contradict each other. Sales can draft, but a single person should confirm anything that makes a promise: notification windows, retention periods, certifications and insurance limits.

Should I send my SOC 2 report instead of filling in the questionnaire?

Sometimes a report or a trust page answers most of it, and many customers accept that for the rows it covers. Ask which rows still need an answer. Whether they accept it is the customer's decision, so do not assume it.

    Read this first

      What it does, and what it leaves to you

      • Finds: the closest saved answer for each question, using weighted term similarity after folding synonyms (MFA, 2FA and multi-factor are one control). Marks each as strong, review or no match, tags the topic and whether it expects yes/no, a list or a description, and spots repeated questions.
      • Flags: figures that differ from the saved answer (24 hours against 72), negated questions, and answers with no figure when one is asked for.
      • Not decided: whether a saved answer is still true, whether it is complete for this customer, or what you may promise. Even a strong match is a suggestion. Every exported row is marked Review. It writes no new answers and makes no compliance claim for you.

      Prefer the command line? node cli.mjs questions.csv --library answers.csv > filled.csv runs the same code on your own machine (see the README in the repository).

      Common questions

      What is a security questionnaire?

      A security questionnaire is a spreadsheet or portal form a customer's security or procurement team sends before buying software. It asks, often in hundreds of rows, how the vendor handles encryption, access control, incident response, backups, subprocessors and compliance. Common formats include SIG, CAIQ and customer-written lists. Most rows repeat across customers, which is why a saved answer library saves so much time.

      How does the matcher choose an answer?

      It compares each incoming question with the questions in your own answer library using term weighting (TF-IDF cosine similarity) after folding common synonyms, so multi-factor, 2FA and MFA count as one control. A strong match is a close paraphrase, a review match is related but not certain, and no match means you write a new answer.

      Why does it flag some strong matches?

      A text match can be the wrong answer. If the new question asks for 24 hours and the saved answer says 72, or one question is negated and the other is not, the row is downgraded to review and the reason is written in the Flags column.

      Is my answer library uploaded?

      No. Matching runs in your browser. The library stays in the page unless you press Save library on this device, which stores it in your browser's local storage; you can clear it any time. There is also a command-line version that runs on your own machine.

      Does it write answers for me?

      No. It reuses answers you have already written and approved, and lists the questions that have none. Every answer in the export is marked Review, because you remain responsible for what you tell a customer.

// Fictional "Acme Notes" answers and a fictional customer questionnaire.
// Nothing here describes a real company's controls.
export const SAMPLE_LIBRARY = `question,answer,tags
Do you require multi-factor authentication for all employee accounts?,Yes. Acme Notes enforces MFA on every employee account through our identity provider.,access
Is customer data encrypted at rest?,Yes. Customer data is encrypted at rest with AES-256.,encryption
Is data encrypted in transit?,Yes. All traffic uses TLS 1.2 or higher.,encryption
How often do you perform penetration tests?,An independent firm tests the application once a year and after major releases.,pentest
Do you have an incident response plan?,Yes. The plan is reviewed yearly and exercised in a tabletop test.,incident
Within how many hours will you notify customers of a security incident?,We notify affected customers within 72 hours of confirming an incident.,incident
Do you perform background checks on employees?,Yes. All employees are screened before their start date where the law allows.,people
Do you maintain backups and test restores?,Daily encrypted backups are kept for 30 days and a restore is tested every quarter.,continuity
Do you use subprocessors that handle customer data?,Yes. The current list is published on our trust page and customers are told before changes.,vendors
Do you have a SOC 2 Type II report?,Yes. A report is available under NDA.,compliance
`;

export const SAMPLE_QUESTIONS = `1.1 Is multi-factor authentication enforced for all staff?
1.2 Describe how customer data is encrypted when stored.

2.3 Do you NOT allow staff to access production data without approval?
